\section[Practice]{Review — four boxes}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-repaso-mandatos}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new. Before the grid: which single box does \textbf{not} use the subjunctive?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{\emph{tú}} & \textbf{\emph{usted}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{do it} & \emph{habla} · \emph{come} & \emph{hable} · \emph{coma} \\
\textbf{don't} & \emph{no hables} · \emph{no comas} & \emph{no hable} · \emph{no coma} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four boxes are the \textbf{subjunctive}, which you built chapters ago for wanting and hoping. The fourth is the ordinary \textbf{he/she present}, which you built long before that.

Now count what this rung actually cost you. A whole grammatical mood — the one every phrasebook opens with — and the only genuinely new material in it was \textbf{eight one-syllable words}: \emph{di, haz, ve, pon, ten, sal, sé, ven}.

Everything else was a form you already owned, doing one more job.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: why the odd box is the odd one}]
It is worth asking why the informal positive command is the exception.

Because it is the one that is said most. \emph{Come}, \emph{ven}, \emph{habla}, \emph{ten} — said to children, friends, dogs, and across kitchens, thousands of times a day for two thousand years. That is the box under the most pressure, and heavy use keeps old short forms alive rather than letting them be replaced by tidier ones.

The same pressure explains the eight irregulars, which live in exactly that box and nowhere else. There are no irregular \emph{negative} commands to learn, because negatives are said less and had time to be regularised.

\textbf{The messiest corner of this grid is the most-used corner.} That has been true of every irregularity in this book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four boxes for \emph{hablar}, then for \emph{comer}
  \item the eight irregulars once more
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of the four boxes use the subjunctive? (\textbf{Three}.) What did this rung genuinely cost? (\textbf{Eight one-syllable words}.) Next: what a command sounds like to the person receiving it.
\end{tcolorbox}
